Thus, with ε now seen to be a very reasonable and normal value instead of much larger number as originally thought, we wonder if any measurements contained errors. The biggest concern here involves the Capacitance reading, as the “12 pF” was not a direct observation, but rather an interpretation by an instrument. The ECE department uses the capacitance meter in question to sort through various wayward capacitors in order to classify them and reuse them in subsequent teaching laboratories. Due to the facts that these laboratories continue to operate with minimal
problems and that seasoned technicians such as Mr. Flasch continue to utilize this device on a regular basis, I would conclude that the capacitance reading is accurate.

Unfortunately, the VHB used in the vertical set-up did not last more than a week and split in half before a capacitance reading could be taken. As a result, no dielectric constant can be deduced at this time.

Also of interest is the fact that only 5.13 kV was applied to the vertical EAP. The fragility of the VHB contributed to low voltage because higher voltages would cut through the material and cause the previously strained polymer to snap back to its un-strained arrangement. The exact “safe” voltage was determined rather crudely by slowly increasing the voltage until the VHB broke and observing any changes present before the failure.
